posts.title: 1.5 million ETH is waiting to start staking.
posts.author: WEB3 Newswire
posts.snippet:
1.5 million ETH is waiting to start staking.

And the queue is now 25 days long.

That's roughly $4 billion worth of ETH sitting in line to become validators on Ethereum.

But there's another queue getting even more attention.

ETH waiting to leave staking exploded from around 166,000 on September 29 to roughly 851,000 by October 2.

That's more than a fivefold jump in three days.

The reason was MetaMask.

After disclosing a security incident, MetaMask began taking affected validators out of service as a precaution. 

MetaMask says it found no evidence that customer wallets or funds were affected.

Around 786,000 ETH was still sitting in the exit queue Monday, worth more than $2 billion.

And Ethereum doesn't let everyone leave at once.

The network currently limits both entry and exit to roughly 57,600 ETH per day. That's deliberate. 

Sudden mass movements of validators could create security risks.

So now you have something slightly unusual happening.
People wanting to stake are waiting.

People wanting to unstake are also waiting.

The difference is that the exit surge appears largely connected to MetaMask's precautionary validator withdrawals.

Lido expects much of that ETH to eventually come back into staking once the affected validators complete the exit and withdrawal process. 

That could take up to 45 days.

Meanwhile, the entry queue has actually cooled.

It was around 2 million ETH with a 35-day wait in early September.

Now it's 1.5 million.
Still a huge queue.

Just moving in the opposite direction.
For Ethereum, that's the interesting signal.

Demand to stake hasn't disappeared.

But the network is also showing just how slowly billions of dollars can move when validator capacity becomes the bottleneck.

posts.title: "DORA is for banks" was never true, in 2026 it stopped being safe.
posts.author: Sylvio S.
posts.snippet:
"DORA is for banks" was never true, in 2026 it stopped being safe.

The Digital Operational Resilience Act has been fully applicable since 17 January 2025. No transitional period. No transposition window either — it's a regulation, not a directive, so there is no national law to wait for.

Its scope is set by Article 2, not by whether you feel like a financial institution. Payment institutions. E-money institutions. Investment firms. Asset managers, including AIFMs and UCITS managers. MiCA-authorised crypto-asset service providers. Crowdfunding platforms. Trading venues, CCPs, CSDs, credit rating agencies.

A twelve-person payment fintech in Paris sits under the same regulation as BNP Paribas. What differs is calibration, not applicability. Article 4's proportionality principle governs how you meet the obligations, never whether they reach you.

The line I hear most is "we're a microenterprise". That's the one that worries me, because it is half right. Microenterprise status does buy a lighter ICT risk-management framework under Article 16. It does not exempt you from incident reporting, from third-party risk obligations, or from the Register of Information.

The ACPR-AMF Fintech Forum put a number on it in October 2025: 36 of 60 French payment service providers qualify as microenterprises under DORA. All sixty are in scope.

What changed this year isn't the law. It's that the supervisors who spent 2025 letting firms settle have opened the inspection cycle they always said they would. No competent authority has publicly confirmed a DORA sanction yet — I wouldn't read that as reassurance. It's the gap between "supervision started" and "first published decision", and that gap closes.

Most of my DORA conversations at Cyber-Management start exactly here.

If you're at a non-bank financial entity: has anyone in your business actually read Article 2 and written down which paragraph catches you?

#DORA #RiskManagement

comments.text: The microenterprise point is the one we flag most to clients too - Article 16's lighter ICT framework has nothing to do with incident reporting timelines under Article 17-19, and that's where we see firms get caught out, especially MiCA-authorised CASPs who assume proportionality covers everything.

From the incident-response side, the gap you describe between 'supervision started' and 'first published decision' is exactly where we see CASPs and payment institutions underinvest - the NIS2/DORA overlap in incident classification alone trips up teams who've only mapped one of the two regimes.

posts.title: Crypto security losses just crossed another uncomfortable milestone.
posts.author: Jetso Analin
posts.snippet:
Crypto security losses just crossed another uncomfortable milestone.

The third quarter of 2026 ended with approximately $1.26 billion lost to crypto hacks and security incidents, according to CertiK.

And one incident played a major role in pushing the number there.

Bitget: $387.5M

On September 24, Bitget detected unauthorized transfers from parts of its hot and warm wallet infrastructure.

The exchange initially estimated the impact at $351.6 million.

That figure was later revised to approximately $387.5 million after additional assets on Zcash and TRON were included in the accounting. Bitget says its cold wallets and private keys were not compromised.

But the bigger story is what happened around the breach.

Bitget's investigation found that attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party security product, obtained internal credentials and used them to forge withdrawal commands that bypassed existing risk controls.

In other words, the attack did not simply involve someone obtaining a private key and draining a wallet.

It moved through the infrastructure surrounding the wallet.

And thats becoming an increasingly important distinction in crypto security.

The Bitget incident accounted for roughly 31% of Q3s total security losses, according to CertiK.

But it wasnt alone.

The quarter also included the approximately $319 million Liquid Network exploit, along with major incidents involving Tectonic and Coldcard. CertiK recorded 247 security incidents during Q3, compared with 219 in Q2.

September was particularly severe.

CertiK recorded approximately $769 million in losses across 99 incidents, making it the largest monthly loss total of 2026 so far.

And this is where the numbers become more interesting than the headline.

Crypto security is no longer just about:
Are the private keys safe?

The attack surface now stretches across:
• Wallet infrastructure
• Transaction authorization systems
• Smart contracts
• Cross-chain protocols
• Third-party software
• Internal credentials
• Backend services
• Access controls
• Risk and verification mechanisms

As more financial activity moves onchain, more infrastructure is being built around those assets.

And every additional layer creates another potential point of failure.

Thats perhaps the biggest lesson from Q3.

The security of digital assets is increasingly dependent on the security of the systems that sit around them.

A blockchain can make transactions transparent and immutable.

But the infrastructure deciding which transaction gets authorized in the first place still needs to withstand sophisticated attacks.

With $1.26 billion lost in a single quarter, that infrastructure layer is becoming impossible to ignore.

#CryptoSecurity #Bitget #CertiK #WalletBreach #FinancialInfrastructure #DigitalAssets #CryptoHacks
posts.reason: In-depth analysis of Q3 2026 crypto security breaches and evolving attack surfaces speaks directly to CISOs, insurers and exchanges under NIS2/DORA scope seeking forensic understanding.

comments.text: The shift CertiK's data points to is real: attackers are increasingly targeting the authorization layer rather than keys directly, which means tracing has to start with the forged withdrawal pattern, not just the destination addresses. In our experience the first few hours after such a breach, before funds hit mixers or cross-chain bridges, determine whether choke-point freezes at exchanges are even possible.

Does CertiK's methodology separate losses recovered or frozen post-incident from gross losses, or is $1.26B purely the initial exposure before any clawback? That distinction matters a lot for assessing real economic damage.

We've seen the same pattern in several cases: a third-party integration gets compromised, internal credentials get lifted, and the withdrawal looks completely legitimate to monitoring systems because it follows the normal authorization flow. It's a much harder forensic problem than a classic key compromise.

🚩 最近の不正アクセス事案の増加。「今」データが悪用されてないだけかも
＜English follows＞

最近、日本国内で不正アクセス事案の報道が急増しています。 

その一方で、多くの企業が「個人情報の漏洩は確認されていない」と説明しています。

もちろん、それは良いニュースです。 

しかし、本当に安心して良いのでしょうか。 

✳️近年、セキュリティ業界で警戒されているのが Harvest Now, Decrypt Later（今収集し、後で解読する） という攻撃シナリオです。 

攻撃者は、今すぐ悪用できない暗号化データや機密情報を収集し、将来の計算能力向上や量子コンピュータの実用化を見据えて保管します。 

つまり、 

「漏洩していない」ではなく、 

「まだ悪用されていないだけ」 

という可能性も考慮する必要があります。 

これから求められるのは、侵入防御だけではありません。 

データを暗号化し、その暗号鍵を適切に保護・管理することです。 

暗号化の強度は、鍵管理の強度によって決まります。 

万が一データが取得されても、鍵が守られていればリスクを大幅に低減できます。 

だからこそ、データ保護・暗号化・鍵管理・シークレット管理・ポスト量子暗号への準備を一体で考えるべき時代が到来しています。暗号化だけでは十分ではなく、集中管理された鍵管理とライフサイクル管理が重要だと主張されています。 

数年後に後悔しないために。 

今こそ、「侵入されるか」ではなく、 

「侵入されてもデータを守れるか」 という視点でセキュリティを見直してみませんか。 

 🔏 現在保有している機密データのうち、5年後、10年後も機密性を維持する必要があるデータは何ですか？ 
 🔏 自社の暗号化データが取得された場合、攻撃者が将来的に復号できない根拠はありますか？ 
 🔏 暗号鍵はどこで生成・保管・運用され、誰が管理していますか？ 
 🔏 鍵管理は各システムごとに分散していますか、それとも一元管理されていますか？  🔏 Harvest Now, Decrypt Laterリスクを自社の経営リスクとして評価したことはありますか？ 
 🔏 量子コンピュータ時代に向けた暗号移行（Crypto Agility）の準備はどこまで進んでいますか？

 🚩 The Rise of Cyber Intrusions: Maybe Your Data Isnt Being Misused… Yet

Reports of unauthorized access incidents continue to increase across Japan. 

In many cases, organizations state that no personal data leakage has been confirmed. 

While that sounds reassuring, is it enough? 

Cybercriminals do not always exploit stolen data immediately. 

 ✳️ One growing concern is the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack model. 

Attackers can steal encrypted data today and store it for future use. 

As computing power advances and quantum technologies mature, data that is protected today may become vulnerable tomorrow. 

The real risk may not be current misuse. 

The real risk may be long-term exposure. 

This is why organizations must think beyond breach prevention. 

Protecting sensitive information requires more than encryption alone. 

Strong cryptographic key protection, centralized key management, and secrets management are equally important. 

The cybersecurity question is no longer: 

Can we stop every intrusion? 

It is: 

Can we protect our data even after an intrusion occurs? 

Now is the time to evaluate long-term data protection strategies and prepare for emerging quantum-era threats. 

 🔏 Which data assets must remain confidential for the next 5 to 10 years? 
 🔏 If encrypted data were stolen today, what prevents future decryption? 
 🔏 How are cryptographic keys generated, stored, and protected? 
 🔏 Is key management centralized or fragmented across multiple systems? 
 🔏 Has your organization assessed the risks of Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks?

comments.text: Freezing 25 wallets is the easier half of this - the harder question is whether those wallets interacted with VASPs that will actually comply with a freeze request once funds have already layered through multiple hops. On 28 September, the City of London Police warned that victims lost more than £101 million to payment-diversion fraud during the last financial year. Report Fraud
For businesses, the lesson is uncomfortable but important.
Fraudsters do not always need to invent a company, forge an entire identity or use an obviously suspicious email address.
Sometimes they compromise a genuine account.
The message may come from a real supplier, adviser, colleague or client. It may refer to a genuine transaction. It may contain the right names, documents and commercial context.
Only the payment instruction is false.
That is why effective fraud prevention cannot rely solely on whether an email “looks right”.
Material changes to bank details, urgent transfers, loan redemptions, property completions and unusually timed payment requests should be verified through an independently sourced channel—not the telephone number or contact details contained in the instruction itself.
At JYY Global, we also look at what happens when prevention fails:
Who ultimately controlled the receiving account?
Which companies, individuals and assets are connected?
Where did the funds move next?
Is the incident isolated, or part of a wider pattern?
What intelligence can support recovery, litigation or a criminal referral?
That may require a combination of corporate intelligence, OSINT, enhanced due diligence, link analysis, asset tracing and targeted investigative enquiries.
Because a familiar name, genuine account or convincing explanation is not independent verification.
Fraud prevention must test the instruction—not simply trust the inbox.

posts.title: Organized crime in South Korea—locally known as jopok (조폭) or geondal—operates through fragmented networks, traditional racketeering, and a modern shift toward high-tech digital an
posts.author: Ibrahim Sîvan Delzell Borjigin
posts.snippet:
Organized crime in South Korea—locally known as jopok (조폭) or geondal—operates through fragmented networks, traditional racketeering, and a modern shift toward high-tech digital and financial scams.
Structure and Operations
• Fragmented Syndicates: Unlike traditional centralized mafias, South Korean organized crime is split into regional and rival factions (such as the Chilsung-pa or Beomseobangpa) rather than a single national syndicate.
• Traditional Activities: Historically and presently, groups engage in extortion, loan sharking, illegal gambling, prostitution, and human trafficking in entertainment districts.
• Absence of Firearms: Due to South Korea's extremely strict gun control laws and severe penalties (often 10+ years for possession), gangs rarely use firearms. Violent disputes typically involve knives or blunt objects like wooden bats.
The Rise of "MZ Gangs"
• Millennial and Gen Z Shift: Recent law enforcement data highlights the emergence of "MZ gangs," comprised of younger generations who bypass traditional rigid hierarchies.
• Digital and Financial Crimes: These newer groups focus less on physical street-level protection rackets and more on crypto scams, credit card fraud, illegal online lottery sites, and voice-phishing or cyber-scams.
Law Enforcement and State Response
• Aggressive Crackdowns: The South Korean National Police Agency routinely executes large-scale operations, arresting thousands of gang members in sweeping multi-city raids.
• Financial Forfeiture: The judiciary heavily targets illicit proceeds through strict asset confiscation and money laundering laws to strip syndicates of their financial motives.
• Limited State Capture: Unlike in some nations, organized crime in South Korea maintains a low political profile and does not exert significant control over government or institutional processes.
posts.reason: Law enforcement perspective on organized crime's shift to crypto scams is relevant to Bloctopus's regulatory and public-sector audience, though it lacks actionable takeaways.

comments.text: The shift you describe toward MZ gangs running crypto scams and voice-phishing fits a pattern we see globally - younger operators treat laundering as a technical problem to be engineered around rather than a risk to be managed, which actually makes the money trail more traceable if you move fast before it's layered across chains.

Given the aggressive asset forfeiture regime you mention, do Korean courts generally accept blockchain-based tracing evidence for freezing orders, or does it still need to be converted into conventional banking-style documentation first?

We've noticed the same generational split in the crypto fraud cases we trace - the proceeds from these MZ-style scams often move through exchanges with weaker KYC in neighboring jurisdictions before hitting a choke point, which is usually the window where tracing actually has a realistic chance.

posts.title: Notice the headline about the Microsoft account on “X” being “hacked” to promote a crypto currency branded as “Clippy”?
posts.author: Gary Longsine
posts.snippet:
Notice the headline about the Microsoft account on “X” being “hacked” to promote a crypto currency branded as “Clippy”?

When I help clients recover from ransomware, cyber extortion, or other network breaches, one thing I recommend is that the company inventory and review the accounts they maintain for social media and access to vendor services.

Who has access to the account credentials?

Where are they stored?

Is each account secured by a unique, long password (at least 15 characters recommended by NIST)?

Is MFA enabled?

Are the account recovery options set up? (Verified phone, verified email, account recovery keys generated and stored in a secure place?)

You really want to review this stuff as soon as possible.

comments.text: Account recovery options are the piece most inventories skip - an attacker who controls a verified recovery phone or email can regain access even after passwords and MFA are reset, so that checklist item deserves equal weight to the password and MFA questions.

In ransomware and extortion cases we're brought into, the social media and vendor-portal angle often gets treated as secondary to the core network breach, but it's frequently where the extortion pressure or reputational damage actually plays out first.

posts.title: A Dutch commodity company came to us for a licence.
posts.author: Andreea Daescu
posts.snippet:
A Dutch commodity company came to us for a licence.
That turned out to be the smallest part of the job.

They were already trading worldwide and wanted Dubai as their hub for the Middle East and Asia. An office, a team, banking, logistics, all close to their customers.

One core product was ethanol. That single detail changed everything, because ethanol is regulated and needs external approval from the UAE police.

So before any licence application, we had to build the whole setup around how the business actually worked:

1. The activity had to reflect what they actually sold

2. Police approval had to be coordinated first

3. Foreign corporate documents were needed, since the parent company was a shareholder

4. Resolutions had to be attested and legalised

5. Banking, corporate tax, office space and a local team all had to follow
The bank alone wanted the full picture.

What they sold, who bought it, where the goods moved, how the money moved.

The group structure, their Netherlands employees, the source of funds behind the beneficial owners.

The company was established. Police approval came through. Banking and corporate tax were completed.

They are still operating from that Dubai hub today.

A regional hub is never just a licence.

It is the activity, the approvals, the banking, the tax, the office and the people, all built around how the business actually works.
posts.reason: Real case study on international business setup with detailed source-of-funds due diligence and banking compliance is highly relevant to lawyers and compliance officers who handle similar structures.

comments.text: The bank wanting the full picture - buyer, goods movement, money movement - is consistent with what we see on the source-of-funds side generally: regulated-goods trades draw far more scrutiny on the money trail than the licence itself ever does.
Did the police approval process for the ethanol activity also require ongoing reporting once operational, or was it a one-time gate at setup?
We run into the same sequencing issue often - clients treat the licence as the finish line, when in practice the banking and source-of-funds documentation ends up being the longer, harder path.

posts.title: Climate finance has a comprehensibility problem. This matters because there is political pressure to cut climate finance commitments.
posts.author: Sam Woodbridge
posts.snippet:
Climate finance has a comprehensibility problem. This matters because there is political pressure to cut climate finance commitments. 

Climate finance helps countries to meet the scale of the climate change challenge with a proportionate response. This domain covers mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage. It includes finance that flows internally from national budgets to domestic projects and across borders from development banks to emerging economies. It blends private capital with public resources. It funds long-term development but also tackles acute shocks. We can debate some of these categories. But the fact we can is evidence of fuzziness.

Without a clear view of the purpose and benefits of climate finance, we’re less able to lobby for its protection.

Consider the range in these initiatives: a sea wall in Monrovia; tree planting in Freetown; drought response in Syria; carbon capture in Denmark; early warning systems in Uzbekistan. There are many variables along the pathway to a practical solution that make the overall label less legible.

Cut funding to something amorphous and it will barely register in the public mind except for those who can trace a direct effect. Often, those who can will be in communities that are distant from the decision and the source of the funds. 

If we cannot clearly and consistently connect climate finance to a result that the public can grasp without searching the websites of specialist institutions or taking an evening course in resilient infrastructure, project finance, or nature-based solutions, we cannot easily communicate what is being cut. 

We must figure out a way to clarify and communicate widely the connection between this global commitment and the stuff that gets done in a specific place to address a climate hazard. What are the examples where this has been done well?

posts.title: The most effective crypto scams rarely begin with obviously bad design. They begin with borrowed trust.
posts.author: Serhii Fedyna

The most effective crypto scams rarely begin with obviously bad design. They begin with borrowed trust.

A familiar logo. A copied support account. A domain that differs by one character. Then comes urgency: connect now, verify now, claim now. The attacker wants the user to act before checking what the wallet is actually requesting.

A useful habit is to separate recognition from verification. Do not trust the logo alone. Open important services from a saved bookmark, inspect the exact domain and read every permission before signing. If the request is unexpected or unclear, stop.

This decision point is one reason we are building Noytrix: to help users examine suspicious links, wallets, contracts and messages before they act.

posts.title: I recently got a LinkedIn DM that invited me to go on a crypto podcast from someone claiming to be from a reputable crypto company (Blockworks) that I immediately knew was a scam.
posts.author: Scott Touchton
posts.snippet:
I recently got a LinkedIn DM that invited me to go on a crypto podcast from someone claiming to be from a reputable crypto company (Blockworks) that I immediately knew was a scam.

Here's how I knew it was a scam:
- too few connections for their claimed resume (about 350 connections for a resume that claimed 2+ years at BlockWorks and 2+ years at CoinDesk)
- we had zero mutual connections (this is a small industry and if you've been in crypto for 4+ years like their resume did, we have mutual connections)
- their oldest post was 1 month old so it was newly spun up account
- the posts didn't match their resume experience (posts were technical coding stuff but their job titles were investor relations, etc)

After searching I came across this post from Andrey U. about the same type scam.

The game is that they send a reputable link (Google Meet/Zoom/etc) to get on a call and then the connection gets "bad" and they send you an alternate link which is malware with a wallet drainer.   (See shared screenshot below for more detailed example).

posts.title: A European #terrorist threat is persistent, increasingly decentralised, digitally mediated and less neatly ideological, while simultaneously becoming more entangled with geopolitic
posts.author: Greg Wlodarczyk
posts.snippet:
A European #terrorist threat is persistent, increasingly decentralised, digitally mediated and less neatly ideological, while simultaneously becoming more entangled with geopolitical conflict, organised crime and state-sponsored hybrid activity 

- highlights the 2026 edition of “In Their Eyes: How European Security Services Look at Terrorism and Counter-Terrorism” report recently published by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. 

As its previous edition, the report is based on an analysis of official reports from counter-terrorism and intelligence services across 23 EU Member States, interviews with experts, and news articles. 

From its key findings I noted:

📍 Jihadi terrorism remains the principal terrorist threat. It is the most frequently prioritised threat across 23 EU Member States. 

📍Right-wing extremism (RWE) remains a serious and persistent second-order threat. Ideological boundaries are becoming increasingly blurred. 

📍Anti-government extremism (AGE), nihilistic violent extremism, misogyny/incel milieus and other hybrid or “post-ideological” forms of violent extremism complicate conventional categorisation. 

📍The threat is increasingly characterised by low-complexity attacks that are difficult to detect. 

In relation to #terroristfinancing specifically, I noted (on a very high level):

📌 Most of the focus of MS reports on the financing of terrorism deals with the way foreign-based jihadi terrorist organisations finance themselves. 

📌 TF has been heavily influenced by the war in Gaza, with jihadist organisations exploiting the conflict for financing ends. 

📌 The RWE scene combines a wide variety of more or less traditional financing means due to its proximity to mainstream political circles with most of RWE funding coming from legitimate sources. 

📌 The two main legal means through which individuals finance terrorism are donations (including fundraising via non-profit organisations) and the purchase of goods or services. Donations are increasingly made on crowdfunding platforms.

📌 Apart from donations, terrorism is increasingly financed by businesses such as Salafist fast-food restaurants or retail shops, RWE merchandise, and by AGE fantasy documents (e.g., sale of make-believe documents such as driving licences or vehicle registration plates). 

📌 Terrorist actors also finance their activities illegally, through ongoing criminal endeavours, white-collar crime (especially linked to RWE), or through ransomware as reported more recently. 

📌 For the transfer of funds, financers of terrorism still resort to physical transfers, but overwhelmingly use a combination of both regulated, informal, or crypto-based digital transfer channels. These include using regulated fiat-based digital channels, Informal Value Transfer Systems (especially used by jihadi terrorist networks), and crypto-assets.

posts.title: Five years into the transfer conditions regulations, the amber flag is still the hardest part of the job.
posts.author: Bryan Dickson
posts.snippet:
Five years into the transfer conditions regulations, the amber flag is still the hardest part of the job.
Red is close to binary. You either have the evidence or you do not, and the transfer does not proceed.
Amber is where judgement lives. High-risk or unregulated investments. A fee structure nobody can explain in a sentence. Overseas involvement that does not obviously fit the member's circumstances. None of it proves anything. All of it is enough to require the member to take MoneyHelper guidance first.
Two failure modes, and I see both:
Flag everything, and a safeguard becomes a queue. Members disengage, legitimate transfers stall, and the guidance appointment turns into a box to tick rather than a genuine intervention.
Flag nothing, and you have quietly decided that scam risk is someone else's problem.
The firms getting this right wrote down what amber means to them, applied it the same way every time, and can explain why a particular case landed where it did.
A defensible decision is not always the cautious one. It is the one you can account for.

posts.title: One transaction rarely tells you the full story.
posts.author: Jai Raj Chauhan
posts.snippet:
One transaction rarely tells you the full story. 

A network does.

At ZIGRAM, we often hear the same thing from AML teams in Indonesia: "But the transaction looked normal."
And honestly, it does!
➡️ The amount wasn't unusually high.
➡️ The frequency didn't raise any flags.
➡️ The receiving account looked like any other customer.

Nothing screamed fraud. But connect the dots, and a very different picture shows up.
This is exactly why mule accounts are so hard to catch. They are used to receive, split, move and hide the money from scams, whether it's online gambling, investment fraud, fake loan apps, or social engineering. With instant rails like BI-FAST, QRIS and e-wallets, that money can be gone in minutes.

One account on its own may look perfectly fine. But zoom out, and you may find it shares a device, phone number, IP address or identity with other suspicious accounts.
Looking at transactions one by one is like reading a single page of a book and trying to guess the ending.
So the questions we should be asking are:
- Who is sending money into this account?
- How fast does it leave after it arrives?
- Is this a pass-through pattern?
- Is one device being used across multiple accounts?
- Is the beneficiary linked to earlier cases?
- Is this account part of a larger fraud cluster?

Fraud today is rarely a one-person job. It's organised, well-coordinated and fast. By the time a single transaction raises an alarm, the money may already be several accounts down the chain. Transaction monitoring on its own will miss what link analysis can reveal.

That's why ZIGRAM's transaction monitoring application lets you deploy 500+ rules across scenarios and thresholds aligned with OJK and BI guidelines, giving you a robust system for mule account detection.

Detection is only half the job. Our application also supports regulatory reporting, including filing STRs and SARs.

📌 OJK's POJK No. 8 of 2023 requires financial service providers to run AML/CFT programmes and report suspicious transactions (LTKM), which are filed through PPATK's goAML system. Bank Indonesia applies similar AML/CFT obligations to payment providers and e-wallets, and reporting parties must submit an STR within 3 working days of detecting a suspicious transaction.

At ZIGRAM this is the conversation we want to have with banks, fintechs and e-wallet providers across Indonesia. Fraud doesn't stay inside one institution, so our defences shouldn't either.

I'd love to hear how your team is approaching mule account detection today. 

#frauddetection #ZIGRAM #OJK #BankIndonesia #AML

Nous avons rejoué l'intégralité du corpus — désormais 2 012 cas gelés (1 161 scams, 849 clean) — avec le moteur en production. Chaque cas a été évalué deux fois : déterminisme parfait, 4 024 évaluations identiques.

🔎 Pipeline complet : ML + faits durs + cap d'innocence GNN

Sur les 1 161 scams :
➡️ 1 153 détectés
➡️ 99,3 % de rappel (97,8 % directement en BLOCK)
➡️ 8 manqués — les cas les plus durs : victimes résolues comme telles, et scams à topologie indiscernable sans faits externes

Côté clean :

➡️ bruit opérationnel : 5,7 % (il était de 17,8 % sur le corpus précédent — divisé par 3)

Sans cap d'innocence : 134 clean en INVESTIGATE
Avec cap : 48
➡️ −86 faux positifs (−64 % du bruit résiduel)
➡️ 0 scam perdu — la distribution des verdicts scam est strictement identique

Le GNN ne vote pas dans le score. Il sert uniquement de canal d'exonération structurelle : quand la topologie dit « structure saine », le moteur rabat le verdict sans jamais toucher aux scams.

Les faits durs apportent +12,3 points de rappel — ils portent le passage en BLOCK, la structure porte le filet zero-day.

🆕 Ce qui a changé depuis la dernière mesure

Le moteur est maintenant auto-audité. Un second modèle — « l'ombre » — rejoue chaque scan en parallèle du moteur déterministe et compare sa lecture à la vérité terrain. Résultat : accord avec le curateur humain de 84,6 %, montant à 87 % quand sa confiance calibrée dépasse 0,9.

C'est cette télémétrie qui nous a permis de découvrir et purger un défaut invisible : un détecteur nommait « rug_pull » des adresses qui étaient en réalité des drainers ou de simples wallets — plus de 600 faux nommages corrigés, sans qu'aucun verdict de protection n'ait été compromis.

La confiance affichée est désormais calibrée (régression isotonique) : quand l'ombre dit 90 %, elle a raison dans ~90 % des cas mesurés. Pas de score prétentieux.

Et une dernière métrique qui compte : 0 faux positif « pig butchering » sur les 258 adresses résolues côté victime. Un moteur qui accuse les victimes n'aide personne.

Philosophie inchangée :
Le ML détecte.
Le graphe et les faits observables apportent la preuve.
Et désormais, une seconde lecture surveille la première.

L'objectif reste le même : produire le bon signal, avec suffisamment de contexte pour qu'un analyste comprenne pourquoi une décision est prise.

CTF Tip: In Crypto challenges with a chosen plaintext encryption oracle, do not immediately start reversing every round of a custom cipher. First test whether the encryption is affine over GF(2). Query E(0), E(a), E(b), and E(a ⊕ b) and check whether E(a) ⊕ E(b) ⊕ E(0) = E(a ⊕ b). If this relation consistently holds, the entire cipher may collapse into a single affine transformation. For a 128 bit block cipher, E(0) plus 128 basis vector queries can recover the complete linear map, after which decryption becomes a matrix inversion problem instead of reversing the cipher round by round.

comments.text: The real bottleneck isn't identifying the cross-chain hops themselves, it's timing — once funds clear a bridge and hit a DEX with no KYC, the window to get a freeze request to a centralised exchange before further layering is often a matter of hours, not days.

What's your view on bridges that don't log sufficient on-chain metadata for the destination-chain hop — do you rely on off-chain cooperation from the bridge operator in those cases, or is the trail treated as broken?

We've seen cases where the trail across three chains and two bridges was fully reconstructable, but the case still stalled because the final receiving exchange was in a jurisdiction with no practical cooperation channel — tracing and recovery are genuinely two different problems.

posts.title: Crypto Virtual Asset Reporting: Where Tax Compliance, Blockchain Traceability, Crypto-laundering Risk, & Crypto Carbon Dating Converge Crypto taxation extends far beyond reporting
posts.author: Nazneen N Motafram North American Tax Accountant Tax Accounting Researcher
posts.snippet:
Crypto Virtual Asset Reporting: Where Tax Compliance, Blockchain Traceability, Crypto-laundering Risk, & Crypto Carbon Dating Converge Crypto taxation extends far beyond reporting gains & losses. 

At its core lies the ability to reconstruct economic reality through immutable blockchain evidence. 

I describe this as Crypto Carbon Dating: the use of blockchain timestamps, transaction hashes, wallet histories, and exchange records to establish the provenance, ownership journey, and chronological life cycle of a virtual asset.

From both the U.S. IRS & Canadian CRA perspectives, the same blockchain evidence forms the foundation of tax compliance. 

While the IRS generally applies property-based tax principles & the CRA applies property or commodity-based treatment, both rely upon reconstructing transaction histories to determine taxable events and reporting obligations.

This same traceability also exposes crypto-laundering. Attempts to obscure illicit funds through mixers, wallet hopping, layering, or cross-chain transfers still leave a permanent blockchain trail. Crypto Carbon Dating enables regulators, forensic accountants, and law enforcement agencies to trace funds back to their origin, identify ownership patterns, & detect suspicious activity.

Thus, one blockchain transaction trail simultaneously supports tax compliance, anti-money laundering enforcement, forensic investigations, audit verification, and regulatory governance. 

As global frameworks such as the OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) mature, blockchain is evolving from a disruptive financial technology into a powerful global compliance infrastructure.

One Blockchain. One Evidence Trail. Multiple Regulatory Outcomes. 

The future of crypto regulation will not be defined by the asset itself, but by our ability to trace, verify, and interpret its immutable digital history.
posts.reason: Expert-level post on blockchain traceability, tax compliance, and crypto-AML enforcement that speaks directly to regulators, compliance officers, and forensic professionals—exactly our target audience.

comments.text: Worth noting that the provenance chain is only as strong as the off-chain attribution linking a wallet to a taxpayer — the blockchain timestamp proves the transaction happened, but establishing who controlled the wallet at that moment still usually depends on exchange KYC records or other external evidence.

With CARF rollout, how do you see jurisdictions handling wallets that show clear laundering-pattern hops (mixer, then cross-chain, then CEX) but where the taxable event itself occurred years before the obfuscation attempt?

In forensic engagements we routinely use exactly this kind of chronological reconstruction, and the hardest part is rarely the technical trail — it's presenting wallet-history evidence in a form a court or tax authority unfamiliar with blockchain mechanics can actually rely on.
